claims.text: Copper selectively segregates to the surface of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Surface copper enrichment lowers the local melting point at the nanoparticle surface.
The locally depressed surface melting point initiates premelting before bulk melting.
Pre-annealing enhances atomic homogenization and suppresses copper surface segregation.
Suppressing copper segregation produces a sharper, higher-temperature melting transition.
The initially synthesized nanoparticles are solid solutions.
Rapid quenching produces a random distribution of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu in the nanoparticles.
Annealing at 600–700 °C in an inert atmosphere promotes atomic homogenization.
During high-temperature exposure, copper segregates toward the surface of rapid-quenched particles.
Copper is the lower-melting constituent relevant to formation of a locally low-melting interface.
Pre-annealing maintains more bulk-like solid-solution behavior during melting.
Rapid-quenched nanoparticles with pronounced surface copper segregation will begin premelting at lower temperatures than pre-annealed, homogenized nanoparticles.
Premelting in copper-segregated particles will appear as a liquid-like surface veneer.
Pre-annealed nanoparticles will display a delayed and sharper melting transition resembling bulk behavior.
The proposed mechanism applies to typical nanoparticle size ranges under controlled inert-atmosphere heating.
Significant secondary-phase formation or extreme particle-size effects may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Rapid atomic interdiffusion during heating may make differences in melting onset and surface segregation subtle.
Thermal gradients in in situ experiments may influence the observed melting behavior.

contradictions.description: The material_initial_state says rapid quenching produces a random elemental distribution, whereas the intervention and baseline say rapid quenching retains or produces elemental segregation. The rapid-quenched baseline is therefore characterized inconsistently.
